tagline: Inland from Grand Marais to the border lakes, and back.
intro: Out of Grand Marais, County Road 12 leaves Lake Superior and heads inland 57 miles, north, then up the Brule River and Swamper Creek and west past Poplar and Birch and Loon lakes, to Saganaga Lake on the Ontario line. There the road ends, and the way back is the way you came.

It began as a footpath from the inland lakes down to Lake Superior and became a dirt road in the 1890s for the Paulson Mine. Pavement reached Hungry Jack Lake by 1957, and the last gravel was paved over in 1979. The name comes from Gunflint Lake, where the Ojibwa and French explorers found chert that throws sparks.

moments.title: Pincushion Mountain
moments.text: A three-mile drive and a nine-mile walk out and back reach the peak, which looks over the Sawtooth Mountains to the harbor and lighthouse of Grand Marais.

moments.title: Hungry Jack Lake
moments.text: Named, so the story goes, for a surveyor's assistant who ran out of food here for a while.

moments.title: Saganaga Lake
moments.text: The end of the road. The Ojibwe called it the Lake of Many Islands, 280 feet at its deepest, and the old Chik-Wauk Lodge, now a museum, looks over it.

practical: The trail is a dead end at Saganaga Lake. Allow at least two hours, since the return to Grand Marais is by the same road.
